prompt: In a B-Tree of minimum degree t, what is the maximum number of keys a non-root node may hold?
explanation: A node with 2t − 1 keys is 'full'. Any more would violate the invariant, which is why insert must split full nodes before descending into them.

prompt: In a B-Tree, how does the height ever increase?
explanation: Only by splitting a full root (which has no parent to absorb its median) — a brand-new root is created with just that one key. This is the only way height grows.

prompt: In a B-Tree, how does the height ever decrease?
acceptedAnswers: when a merge empties the root
explanation: Only when a merge consumes the root's last remaining key (root had 1 key, both children had t−1) — the merged node becomes the new root, and height decreases by one.

prompt: [Lecture example] Starting from a B-Tree of degree t=2 with root [9,40] and children [2,4,5], [12,15,30], [55,60,69], insert 67, 45, 13, 56 in that order. What are all keys in the final tree, sorted ascending?
explanation: All 11 original keys plus the 4 inserted ones (67, 45, 13, 56) remain present — a B-Tree never loses keys on insert, it only restructures via splits.

prompt: [Lecture example] Starting from a B-Tree of degree t=3 with root [16], left child [3,7,13] (children [1,2],[4,5,6],[10,11,12],[14,15]) and right child [20,23] (children [17,18,19],[21,22],[24,25]), delete 6, 13, 7, 4 in that order. What are all keys remaining, sorted ascending?
explanation: 6 is removed directly from a leaf with keys to spare. 13 is replaced by its predecessor 12. 7 forces a merge of its two t−1-key children. 4 forces the root's two t−1-key children to merge (root shrinks by one level), then descends into the now-merged node.
